units.section: INTRO
units.spoken: Direct Preference Optimization (DPO)

units.section: INTRO
units.spoken: Train on people's preferences directly, with no separate scorer and no trial-and-error loop.

units.section: INTRO
units.spoken: This page builds on RL Basics and Aligning Language Models with RL. The terms below are the ones this page keeps using.

units.section: INTRO
units.spoken: 1. An agent is the learner that picks the moves. A state is the agent's situation right now; a move, or action, is one choice the agent can make in a state; a reward is the number the world hands back after each move, good or bad.

units.section: INTRO
units.spoken: 2. A token is a word or a piece of a word; a language model writes its reply one token at a time.

units.section: INTRO
units.spoken: 3. Here the agent is the language model. Here the state is the prompt plus the tokens written so far, and the move is the next token. Here the reward is one number for the whole reply, given when the reply ends.

units.section: INTRO
units.spoken: 4. RL, short for reinforcement learning, is learning which moves to make from rewards rather than from labelled answers.

units.section: INTRO
units.spoken: 5. A policy is the agent's rule for choosing a move in each state; it may always pick the same move or pick by chance. The policy is the language model being trained to write replies.

sections.section: 1 Why the usual route is slow and costly

units.section: 1 Why the usual route is slow and costly
units.spoken: Section one, Why the usual route is slow and costly

units.section: 1 Why the usual route is slow and costly
units.spoken: DPO learns from fixed preference pairs

units.section: 1 Why the usual route is slow and costly
units.spoken: What. Picture a person reading two summaries of one post and picking the better one. DPO, direct preference optimization, learns straight from such pairs, with no separate scorer and no fresh replies written while it trains.

units.section: 1 Why the usual route is slow and costly
units.spoken: How. It trains on fixed pairs, raising the chosen summary's chance and lowering the rejected one's.

units.section: 1 Why the usual route is slow and costly
units.spoken: Why. When it works, the model writes replies people prefer, learned from picks alone.

units.section: 1 Why the usual route is slow and costly
units.spoken: Training a language model from people's preferences the usual way, RLHF, reinforcement learning from human feedback, is slow and costly, because it keeps writing fresh replies while it trains. The usual route and the RL route are two names this page uses for that same method.

units.section: 1 Why the usual route is slow and costly
units.spoken: The running example is Reddit TL;DR, a set of Reddit posts with a short summary written underneath. A model writes two summaries of one post, and the task is to say which summary is better.

units.section: 1 Why the usual route is slow and costly
units.spoken: One example carries the whole page. The roommate post and its two summaries follow DPO from the pair to the loss to its failure.

units.section: 1 Why the usual route is slow and costly
units.spoken: Take a look at this figure. One post, two summaries, and the better one marked. The post sits on top, Summary 1 says what happened and what the owner asks, and Summary 2 only says someone has a roommate and leftovers. The lesson is the pick: a person chose Summary 1, and that pick is the label DPO learns from.

units.section: 1 Why the usual route is slow and costly
units.spoken: Figure 1 shows one preference pair: the roommate post with two summaries, and the better one marked. The post sits on top, Summary 1 says what happened and what the owner asks, Summary 2 only says someone has a roommate and leftovers, and the mark names Summary 1 better. Take the roommate post: a person picked Summary 1 over Summary 2, and that pick is the label DPO learns from.

units.section: 1 Why the usual route is slow and costly
units.spoken: 1.1The usual route trains a scorer first

units.section: 1 Why the usual route is slow and costly
units.spoken: The scorer first

units.section: 1 Why the usual route is slow and costly
units.spoken: What. Picture the usual route: a scorer is trained on people's picks first, then the model writes fresh replies and is pushed toward high scores. A reward model is a language model with a one-number output, trained so the reply people preferred scores higher.

units.section: 1 Why the usual route is slow and costly
units.spoken: How. Each pair teaches the scorer one comparison: the chosen reply scores higher than the rejected one.

units.section: 1 Why the usual route is slow and costly
units.spoken: Why. When it works, the scorer turns people's picks into a number training can chase.

units.section: 1 Why the usual route is slow and costly
units.spoken: The RL loop

units.section: 1 Why the usual route is slow and costly
units.spoken: What. Picture the model writing fresh replies, scoring them, updating. RLHF trains the policy with PPO, proximal policy optimization, the usual RL method for language models.

units.section: 1 Why the usual route is slow and costly
units.spoken: How. A critic, a second network that predicts the score each partial reply will end with, helps PPO. Training starts from SFT, supervised fine-tuning, trained on replies people wrote with the ordinary next-token loss. A reference model, a frozen copy of the SFT model, holds the policy close with a KL penalty: KL measures how different two probability distributions are, zero when they match.

units.section: 1 Why the usual route is slow and costly
units.spoken: Why. When it works, the policy writes replies that score high and stay readable, at the cost of a scorer to train, fresh replies to write, and a critic.

units.section: 1 Why the usual route is slow and costly
units.spoken: The loss needs no guess of how a partial summary will score, because it compares whole summaries.

units.section: 1 Why the usual route is slow and costly
units.spoken: Only the policy and the frozen reference sit in memory.

units.section: 1 Why the usual route is slow and costly
units.spoken: Take a look at this figure. Two routes from the same pairs, side by side. The left route trains a scorer, runs an RL loop and writes fresh replies. The right route runs the pairs through one loss with a frozen reference. The lesson is what DPO drops: no scorer to train, no fresh replies, no RL loop.

units.section: 1 Why the usual route is slow and costly
units.spoken: Figure 2 sets the two routes side by side: the RLHF column trains a scorer, runs an RL loop and writes fresh replies, while the DPO column runs the pairs through one loss with a frozen reference. The left column stacks boxes from pairs to fresh replies, and the right column stacks boxes from pairs to a trained policy, ending in a dashed box that says no reward model and no RL loop. Take the roommate pair: the left route would score fresh summaries and run RL on them, while the right route trains on the pair as it stands.

sections.section: 2 The policy already carries a reward

units.section: 2 The policy already carries a reward
units.spoken: Section two, The policy already carries a reward

units.section: 2 The policy already carries a reward
units.spoken: DPO's key result is that the policy itself carries a reward for every reply.

units.section: 2 The policy already carries a reward
units.spoken: Take the roommate pair: each summary carries an implicit reward, how much more the policy likes it than the reference does. Each summary's reward is positive when the policy likes it more than the reference does, and negative when it likes it less.

units.section: 2 The policy already carries a reward
units.spoken: For any reward, the policy that earns the most reward minus the KL penalty is the reference with each reply boosted by its reward.

units.section: 2 The policy already carries a reward
units.spoken: Closed-form means the best policy can be written down as a formula, with no training loop needed to find it, but the formula needs the true reward and a sum over every possible reply, so it cannot be used directly.

units.section: 2 The policy already carries a reward
units.spoken: Turn that formula around and it reads a reward off any policy, the same implicit reward.

units.section: 2 The policy already carries a reward
units.spoken: So one supervised loss, a loss on fixed pairs with known picks, can train the policy.

sections.section: 3 From the KL objective to a loss that compares pairs

units.section: 3 From the KL objective to a loss that compares pairs
units.spoken: Section three, From the KL objective to a loss that compares pairs

units.section: 3 From the KL objective to a loss that compares pairs
units.spoken: An expected value is the average over everything that can happen by chance, weighted by how likely each outcome is.

units.section: 3 From the KL objective to a loss that compares pairs
units.spoken: DPO and the RL route both start from the same KL objective.

units.section: 3 From the KL objective to a loss that compares pairs
units.spoken: The pair dataset holds fixed pairs, each one a post with a chosen and a rejected summary.

units.section: 3 From the KL objective to a loss that compares pairs
units.spoken: One post can get many different summaries from the policy.

units.section: 3 From the KL objective to a loss that compares pairs
units.spoken: So Equation 1 scores the summaries the policy actually writes, on the posts it is trained on.

units.section: 3 From the KL objective to a loss that compares pairs
units.spoken: Equation 1. The objective DPO solves. A summarizer trained from people's picks needs a target that rewards summaries people prefer without letting the model drift into text no one would write. A TL;DR model that chases picks alone can drift far from readable English.

units.section: 3 From the KL objective to a loss that compares pairs
units.spoken: Take a look at this equation. A summarizer trained from people's picks needs a target that rewards summaries people prefer without letting the model drift into text no one would write.

units.section: 3 From the KL objective to a loss that compares pairs
units.spoken: The objective line. Max sub thay-ta picks the policy weights that make what follows biggest. E is the expected value, the average over everything that can happen by chance. Ex is one post, drawn from the pair dataset. Dee is the pair dataset, the fixed pairs the model trains on. Why is one summary the policy writes to that post. Pee sub thay-ta is the policy itself, giving each summary its chance. Ar of ex and why is the reward of that summary. Intuitively, the objective is the average reward of the summaries the policy writes.

units.section: 3 From the KL objective to a loss that compares pairs
units.spoken: Intuition. The objective scores what the policy writes, so the best policy is the one whose summaries earn the most reward.

units.section: 3 From the KL objective to a loss that compares pairs
units.spoken: Example. Take the roommate post: a post the dataset draws often counts more in the outer sum, and a summary the policy writes often counts more in the inner sum.

units.section: 3 From the KL objective to a loss that compares pairs
units.spoken: The drift line. Beta is the KL penalty strength, setting the price of drifting. K L is the drift between the two reply distributions, the policy's reply chances and the reference's. Pee sub thay-ta is the policy's chance of each reply to the post. Pee sub ref is the reference's chance of the same reply. The minus sign takes away beta times the drift, so drifting from readable text costs. Intuitively, the reward is not free: drifting costs, and beta sets the price.

units.section: 3 From the KL objective to a loss that compares pairs
units.spoken: Intuition. The reward is not free: drifting from readable text costs, and beta sets the price.

units.section: 3 From the KL objective to a loss that compares pairs
units.spoken: Example. Take the roommate post: raising beta keeps the policy near the reference, so its summaries stay readable, while lowering beta lets it drift further for more reward.

units.section: 3 From the KL objective to a loss that compares pairs
units.spoken: So the objective is the average reward of the summaries the policy writes, minus beta times the drift from the reference.

units.section: 3 From the KL objective to a loss that compares pairs
units.spoken: Its best policy can be written down.

units.section: 3 From the KL objective to a loss that compares pairs
units.spoken: Equation 2. The best policy under the KL penalty. Knowing the target policy matters because DPO never trains a reward model, so the policy itself has to carry the reward. A TL;DR summarizer that starts from supervised fine-tuning already writes readable summaries, and the best policy keeps that starting point in view.

units.section: 3 From the KL objective to a loss that compares pairs
units.spoken: Take a look at this equation. The best policy is the reference, tilted toward high-reward summaries.

units.section: 3 From the KL objective to a loss that compares pairs
units.spoken: The best-policy line. Pee star is the best possible policy, the chance it gives summary why to post ex. Why is one summary, and ex is the post it answers. One over zee of ex divides by the rescaling number, the number that makes all the chances add to one. Pee sub ref is the reference chance of that summary. The equals sign says the right side builds the best policy's chance. Intuitively, the best policy is the reference chance, rescaled so all the chances add to one.

units.section: 3 From the KL objective to a loss that compares pairs
units.spoken: Intuition. The best policy is the reference, tilted toward high-reward summaries.

units.section: 3 From the KL objective to a loss that compares pairs
units.spoken: Example. Take the roommate post: Summary 1's reference chance and Summary 2's are both divided by the same number, so each keeps its share, and the full distribution still adds to one.

units.section: 3 From the KL objective to a loss that compares pairs
units.spoken: The boost line. Exp is the exponential, the function that turns a score into a multiplier. One over beta times the reward divides the reward by beta, so a small beta makes the boost sharp and a large beta makes it gentle. Ar of ex and why is the reward of that summary. The times sign multiplies the rescaled reference chance by the boost. Intuitively, each summary's reference chance is boosted by its reward, more when the reward is high.

units.section: 3 From the KL objective to a loss that compares pairs
units.spoken: Intuition. Each summary's reference chance is boosted by its reward, more when the reward is high.

units.section: 3 From the KL objective to a loss that compares pairs
units.spoken: Example. Take the roommate post: with a small beta the boost gap between Summary 1 and Summary 2 is sharp, and with a large beta both boosts sit near one and the best policy stays near the reference.

units.section: 3 From the KL objective to a loss that compares pairs
units.spoken: So the best policy takes the reference chance of each summary, multiplies it by the exponential boost from its reward, and rescales by zee of ex so all the chances add to one.

units.section: 3 From the KL objective to a loss that compares pairs
units.spoken: Turned around, that formula reads a reward off the policy.

units.section: 3 From the KL objective to a loss that compares pairs
units.spoken: Equation 3. The reward read off the policy. With no reward model to train, the reward has to come from somewhere the policy already carries, and that is what makes direct training possible. A TL;DR model that already prefers the chosen summary over the rejected one carries that preference in how far it moved from its starting point.

units.section: 3 From the KL objective to a loss that compares pairs
units.spoken: Take a look at this equation. The reward is read off how far the policy moved from where it started.

units.section: 3 From the KL objective to a loss that compares pairs
units.spoken: The reward line. Ar of ex and why is the reward of summary why to post ex, read off how far the best policy moved from the reference. Beta scales drift into reward. Log is the logarithm, turning a ratio into a difference. Pee star is the best policy's chance of that summary, on top of the fraction. Pee sub ref is the reference chance, underneath. Above one when the best policy likes a summary more, the log is positive; below one, negative; one when they agree, zero. Intuitively, the reward is beta times the log of how much the policy likes a summary over the reference.

units.section: 3 From the KL objective to a loss that compares pairs
units.spoken: Intuition. The reward is read off how far the policy moved from where it started.

units.section: 3 From the KL objective to a loss that compares pairs
units.spoken: Example. Take the roommate post: the policy likes Summary 1 more than the reference did, so its fraction sits above one and its reward is positive, while Summary 2's sits below one and its reward is negative.

units.section: 3 From the KL objective to a loss that compares pairs
units.spoken: The prompt term line. Beta times the log of zee of ex adds a second term to the reward. Log is the logarithm, and zee of ex is the rescaling number of the post. Zee of ex depends only on the post, so when two summaries of the same post are compared, the same number is added to both and it cancels in the gap. Intuitively, a prompt-only term joins the reward, and it cancels when two summaries are compared.

units.section: 3 From the KL objective to a loss that compares pairs
units.spoken: Intuition. A prompt-only term joins the reward, and it cancels when two summaries are compared.

units.section: 3 From the KL objective to a loss that compares pairs
units.spoken: Example. Take the roommate post: the same zee number joins Summary 1's reward and Summary 2's, so it drops out of the gap between them.

units.section: 3 From the KL objective to a loss that compares pairs
units.spoken: The implicit reward line. Ar hat sub thay-ta is the implicit reward, the hat marking a reward read off the policy. Beta multiplies the log of the fraction: pee sub thay-ta, the trained policy chance, over pee sub ref, the reference. This line carries no zee term, since that term cancels when two summaries of one post are compared. Intuitively, any policy, not just the best one, carries its own reward read the same way.

units.section: 3 From the KL objective to a loss that compares pairs
units.spoken: Intuition. Any policy, not just the best one, carries its own reward read the same way.

units.section: 3 From the KL objective to a loss that compares pairs
units.spoken: Example. Take the roommate post: as training lifts Summary 1's policy chance above its reference chance, its implicit reward climbs past zero.

units.section: 3 From the KL objective to a loss that compares pairs
units.spoken: So a summary's reward is beta times the log of how much the policy likes it over the reference, plus a prompt-only term that cancels.

units.section: 3 From the KL objective to a loss that compares pairs
units.spoken: The reward model loss, the loss the Reward Models page teaches, scores each pair by the gap between the two replies' rewards, and the sigmoid of that gap is the Bradley-Terry chance the chosen summary wins. The sigmoid squashes any number into a chance between zero and one: near one when the chosen summary scores well above the rejected one, near zero when it scores below, and one half when the two scores match. Put the implicit rewards from the card above into that loss, and the part that depends only on the prompt cancels, because both summaries share the same post.

units.section: 3 From the KL objective to a loss that compares pairs
units.spoken: Equation 4. The DPO loss. A pair of summaries with a human pick between them needs a training signal that turns that pick into an update, without writing any new summaries during training. The roommate post with its chosen Summary 1 and rejected Summary 2 is the pair the loss learns from.

units.section: 3 From the KL objective to a loss that compares pairs
units.spoken: Take a look at this equation. The loss turns each human pick into a number training can shrink.

units.section: 3 From the KL objective to a loss that compares pairs
units.spoken: The loss line. El sub dee pee oh of thay-ta is the loss, the number training makes as small as possible, a function of the weights thay-ta. Thay-ta is the policy's weights, the numbers training changes. E is the expected value, the average over the pair dataset. Dee is the pair dataset, the same fixed pairs, each pair one triple of the roommate post ex, the chosen Summary 1 why sub w, and the rejected Summary 2 why sub el. The big square bracket opens the average and closes at the end of the next line. Intuitively, the loss turns each human pick into a number training can shrink.

units.section: 3 From the KL objective to a loss that compares pairs
units.spoken: Intuition. The loss turns each human pick into a number training can shrink.

units.section: 3 From the KL objective to a loss that compares pairs
units.spoken: Example. Take the roommate pair: the average runs over fixed pairs like it, each pair contributing its own negative log chance to the sum.

units.section: 3 From the KL objective to a loss that compares pairs
units.spoken: The pair term line. Log is the logarithm, and sigma is the sigmoid, squashing any number into a chance between zero and one. The bracket holds the score gap: ar hat sub thay-ta of ex and why sub w, the chosen Summary 1's implicit reward, minus ar hat sub thay-ta of ex and why sub el, the rejected one's. That sigmoid is the Bradley-Terry chance the chosen summary wins: a large positive gap gives a chance near one, a large negative gap near zero, and a zero gap one half. Intuitively, a pair counts while the model ranks it wrong, and barely counts once it ranks it right.

units.section: 3 From the KL objective to a loss that compares pairs
units.spoken: Intuition. A pair counts while the model ranks it wrong, and barely counts once it ranks it right.

units.section: 3 From the KL objective to a loss that compares pairs
units.spoken: Example. Take the roommate pair while Summary 1 sits well ahead: the gap is large, the sigmoid chance is near one, and the pair adds almost nothing.

units.section: 3 From the KL objective to a loss that compares pairs
units.spoken: So the loss says this: average the negative log of the sigmoid gap over the pairs, and make it as small as possible.

units.section: 3 From the KL objective to a loss that compares pairs
units.spoken: Its gradient shows how hard each pair pushes.

units.section: 3 From the KL objective to a loss that compares pairs
units.spoken: Equation 5. The gradient weight. A training step should push hard on a pair the model still ranks wrong and barely move on a pair it already ranks right, or learning wastes its steps. The roommate pair, while Summary 2 still sits ahead of Summary 1, is a pair that deserves a hard push.

units.section: 3 From the KL objective to a loss that compares pairs
units.spoken: Take a look at this equation. A training step should push hard on a pair the model still ranks wrong and barely move on a pair it already ranks right.

units.section: 3 From the KL objective to a loss that compares pairs
units.spoken: The gradient line. Nabla sub thay-ta of el sub dee pee oh is the gradient of the loss over the weights thay-ta, the direction, across all the model's weights, that raises the loss fastest. The minus sign flips the direction, so the step raises the chosen summary's log-probability and lowers the rejected one's. Beta multiplies the average that follows, scaling each pair's push. E is the expected value, the average over the fixed pairs. Dee is the pair dataset, the same pairs the loss averages over. The big square bracket opens the average and closes after the push. Intuitively, the gradient points up the loss, and training steps the other way.

units.section: 3 From the KL objective to a loss that compares pairs
units.spoken: Intuition. The gradient points up the loss, and training steps the other way.

units.section: 3 From the KL objective to a loss that compares pairs
units.spoken: Example. Take the roommate pair: with Summary 2 still ahead of Summary 1, its push is large and the step moves hard.

units.section: 3 From the KL objective to a loss that compares pairs
units.spoken: The weight line. Sigma is the sigmoid, squashing any number into a chance between zero and one, and the big round bracket holds the reversed gap: the implicit reward ar hat sub thay-ta of ex and why sub el of the rejected Summary 2 minus the implicit reward ar hat sub thay-ta of ex and why sub w of the chosen Summary 1. The order is reversed from the loss, so the weight is large when the rejected summary has the higher implicit reward and near zero when the chosen summary is well ahead; when the two rewards are equal the weight is one half. Intuitively, the weight is large exactly when the rejected summary still sits ahead.

units.spoken: Intuition. The same step pushes the rejected summary down, by the same weight.

units.section: 3 From the KL objective to a loss that compares pairs

units.section: 3 From the KL objective to a loss that compares pairs
units.spoken: So the whole gradient says this: the average over the fixed pairs of minus beta times the sigmoid weight times the chosen gradient minus the rejected gradient, so each pair pushes the chosen summary up and the rejected one down by how wrong the ranking still is.

units.section: 3 From the KL objective to a loss that compares pairs

units.spoken: The weight line. Sigma of the reversed gap is the weight: the rejected Summary 2's implicit reward, ar hat sub thay-ta of ex and why sub el, minus the chosen Summary 1's, ar hat sub thay-ta of ex and why sub w, passed through the sigmoid. That makes the weight large while the rejected summary still sits ahead and near zero once the chosen summary is well ahead, one half when the two rewards are equal. units.section: 4 One training step on a preference pair
units.spoken: So one step reads the rewards off the policy, turns the gap into a chance, and pushes by the weight: up on the chosen summary, down on the rejected one.

units.section: 4 One training step on a preference pair
units.spoken: 4.1Only the policy trains, on a fixed set of pairs

units.section: 4 One training step on a preference pair
units.spoken: A DPO step computes the loss on a batch, a group of fixed pairs trained on together, and takes one gradient step.

units.section: 4 One training step on a preference pair
units.spoken: One gradient step runs on a batch of fixed pairs like the roommate pair; the reference log-probabilities for each pair are computed once before training.

units.section: 4 One training step on a preference pair
units.spoken: Training runs over a fixed pair dataset, each epoch one full pass over the pairs. The policy trains and the reference stays frozen.

units.section: 4 One training step on a preference pair
units.spoken: Each pair needs two forward passes per model, two runs of the model over a summary to score it, one for the chosen summary and one for the rejected one. The reference runs its two passes once up front; only the policy runs two passes on every step. So only the policy's weights move.

units.section: 5 The DPO loss in PyTorch
units.spoken: Section five, The DPO loss in PyTorch

units.section: 5 The DPO loss in PyTorch
units.spoken: Each summary is scored by its log-probability, the sum of its tokens' log-probabilities, one number per summary, for the policy and the frozen reference. Training makes that loss as small as possible.

units.section: 5 The DPO loss in PyTorch
units.spoken: The code below takes the roommate pair's summed token log-probabilities, policy and reference, and returns the loss, the logged margin and the chosen reward.

units.section: 5 The DPO loss in PyTorch
units.spoken: This code is the DPO loss in PyTorch. It takes the roommate pair's summed token log-probabilities, policy and reference, plus beta, and returns the loss, the logged margin and the chosen reward. The first two lines read the implicit reward of each summary off the policy: beta times the policy log-probability minus the reference log-probability, chosen and rejected. The third line is the loss itself: the negative log of the sigmoid of the gap between the two rewards, averaged over the batch. The fourth line logs the margin, cut loose from the graph so it carries no push back to the policy. The last line also watches the chosen reward: if it falls, the chosen reply is losing chance.

The beta slider moves the bars, and the Pal's case toggle makes both replies look alike. The lesson is the margin: it grows even as both bars fall.

units.section: 7 Training with DPO in practice
units.spoken: Section seven, Training with DPO in practice

units.section: 7 Training with DPO in practice
units.spoken: TRL, Transformer Reinforcement Learning, Hugging Face's open library for training language models with these methods, has a DPO trainer. The paper's authors also published a reference implementation.

units.section: 7 Training with DPO in practice
units.spoken: Because the reference model is frozen, only the policy's scores change during training, which saves memory and time.

units.section: 7 Training with DPO in practice
units.spoken: During training, watch the logged margin and the chosen reward, the implicit reward of the chosen reply, which training libraries log.

units.section: 7 Training with DPO in practice
units.spoken: The learning rate eta sets how big a step each update takes.

units.section: 7 Training with DPO in practice
units.spoken: This table lists the four settings that shape a DPO run and what each one does when it moves. Read across a row to see one setting and its value, and down the Raise and Lower columns to compare the trade-offs. Beta is zero point one by default, zero point five for TL;DR: raising it keeps the policy near the reference, lowering it lets it drift further with more risk. Batch is sixty-four: raising it is steadier, lowering it noisier. Optimizer and learning rate is RMSprop at one times ten to the minus six, which scales each weight's step by how large its recent gradients were: raising it is faster but less stable, lowering it slower. Warmup starts the learning rate near zero and raises it over the first one hundred fifty steps: a steadier start with slower early progress, while skipping it risks early updates overshooting.

units.section: 7 Training with DPO in practice
units.spoken: Table 1 lists the four settings that shape a DPO run and what each one does when it moves. Take beta: raising it keeps the policy near the reference, and lowering it lets the policy drift further for more reward.

units.section: 8 When to choose DPO
units.spoken: Section eight, When to choose DPO

units.section: 8 When to choose DPO
units.spoken: The run that answers this question trained DPO on fixed pairs of summaries and single-turn dialogue replies, one prompt with one reply, the same pairs the RL route used. GPT-4 judged which model's replies won, as a stand-in for people's picks, and the win rate is the share of comparisons a model's replies win. People judged three head-to-head tests against PPO sampled greedily, one each for DPO, SFT, and PPO-1, which is PPO sampled at temperature 1.0, and in the DPO test DPO replies were preferred 58 percent of the time. DPO sampled at temperature 0.25 and PPO at 0, where temperature sets how varied the sampled replies are. A separate test steered replies toward positive sentiment: the model finished the start of a movie review, and a sentiment classifier scored how positive the ending was.

units.section: 8 When to choose DPO
units.spoken: Table 2 compares the two routes: DPO matched the RL route on summaries and single-turn dialogue, and beat it at steering sentiment.

units.section: 8 When to choose DPO
units.spoken: Table 2 compares the two routes across three columns: summaries and single-turn dialogue, steering sentiment, and what each route needed. Read across a row to see one route and what it needed. DPO matched the RL route on summaries and single-turn dialogue, beat it at steering sentiment, and needed no reward model to train, no replies written while training, and little tuning. The RL route was matched by DPO on summaries and dialogue and beaten by DPO on sentiment, and it needed a reward model to train, replies written while training, and more tuning. The lesson is the trade: the same results on summaries and dialogue, better on sentiment, for much less machinery.

units.section: 8 When to choose DPO
units.spoken: 1. You have fixed human or AI preference pairs. DPO trains on the pairs as they are, so it needs nothing beyond them.

units.section: 8 When to choose DPO
units.spoken: 2. Compute is limited. No scorer to train and no RL loop to run.

units.section: 8 When to choose DPO
units.spoken: 3. The task is chat-style alignment. The pairs are replies people judged, and the loss only needs the gap between two replies.

units.section: 8 When to choose DPO
units.spoken: When a program can check the answer, prefer GRPO, group relative policy optimization. Its rule rewards are numbers a program computes.

units.section: 8 When to choose DPO
units.spoken: DPO fits pairs like the roommate pair: fixed pairs judged by a person, not checked by a program.

units.section: 8 When to choose DPO
units.spoken: DPO learns from a fixed dataset of pairs and never from replies the current model just wrote, so it needs no sampling loop, a loop that writes fresh replies to learn from. When the pairs no longer look like the replies the model writes, DPO has nothing fresh to learn from, so refresh the pairs or use a method that writes fresh replies.

sections.section: 9 When the chosen reply gets less likely too

units.section: 9 When the chosen reply gets less likely too
units.spoken: Section nine, When the chosen reply gets less likely too

units.section: 9 When the chosen reply gets less likely too
units.spoken: Likelihood displacement

units.section: 9 When the chosen reply gets less likely too
units.spoken: What. Picture the chosen reply sliding down while the gap still grows: the loss only needs the gap to grow, so both summaries can fall. Likelihood displacement is the name Razin's study gives to the chosen reply becoming less likely during DPO.

units.section: 9 When the chosen reply gets less likely too
units.spoken: How. Plain DPO's loss keeps pushing the margin up without end, so the chosen reply's chance can fall as long as the rejected one falls faster. Two studies split the cause. Pal's case is pairs that differ in only a few words: the push after the differing word drags both replies down. Razin's measure is the CHES score, how alike the two replies are inside the model, judged by their hidden embeddings, the model's inner numbers for each reply.

units.section: 9 When the chosen reply gets less likely too
units.spoken: Why. When it works, the fixes hold the chosen reply up: DPO-Positive adds a penalty whenever the chosen reply becomes less likely than under the reference, filtering drops pairs with a high CHES score, and adding the SFT loss on the chosen reply raises its own chance directly, instead of only widening the gap between the two replies.

units.section: 9 When the chosen reply gets less likely too
units.spoken: Two more fixes cap the margin itself. Label smoothing treats each pick as slightly uncertain, so the loss stops pushing once the margin reaches a set size. IPO, identity preference optimization, aims the loss at a fixed margin instead of an ever larger one.

units.section: 9 When the chosen reply gets less likely too
units.spoken: Take a shortened copy of Summary 1, the same summary with its second clause dropped: "A roommate ate saved leftovers."

units.section: 9 When the chosen reply gets less likely too
units.spoken: Table 3 lines up what breaks DPO, what it looks like, and the fix for each. Read across a row to see one cause, its symptom and its fix, and down the rows to compare the failures. First, the shortened Summary 1 and Summary 2 both fall while the gap grows: the logged chosen reward goes negative while margins rise, and quality can drop, with chance shifting onto replies nobody wanted. The fixes are DPO-Positive, filtering out pairs with a high CHES score, and adding the ordinary SFT loss on the chosen reply. Second, pairs unlike the replies this model writes teach less: pairs written by another model can teach less. The fix is SFT on the chosen replies first, or write pairs with the policy itself. Third, beta too low, or too high: too low, and the policy drifts far from the reference, and the text can degenerate, breaking down into repetition or nonsense. Too high, and it barely moves. Raise beta when it drifts too far, lower it when it barely moves. Fourth, overfitting the margin: training margins sit near their ceiling while the win rate on new pairs stays flat. The fixes are label smoothing and IPO.

units.section: 9 When the chosen reply gets less likely too
units.spoken: With Pal's case on in the tool above, both bars slide down while the gap grows.

sections.section: 10 Back to sampling, without the critic

units.section: 10 Back to sampling, without the critic
units.spoken: Section ten, Back to sampling, without the critic

units.section: 10 Back to sampling, without the critic
units.spoken: What if we keep writing fresh answers and a reward, but drop the critic?

units.section: 10 Back to sampling, without the critic
units.spoken: The next method samples a group of replies to one prompt, scores each one, and compares the scores inside the group. The group's own average is the baseline, and the spread of the scores sets the scale, so no critic network is needed to guess each reply's value. That method is GRPO, group relative policy optimization, and the next page teaches it.

units.section: 10 Back to sampling, without the critic
units.spoken: Sampling without a critic keeps the fresh replies written while training, each with a reward. The critic is a network as big as the model it trains, so leaving it out saves that whole network, and the reward model goes too when a program checks the answer.

units.section: 10 Back to sampling, without the critic
units.spoken: That setup fits where answers can be checked by a program, such as math and code, because a rule reward replaces the learned scorer. Where no program can check, the learned scorer stays.

units.section: 10 Back to sampling, without the critic
units.spoken: The same idea reaches models that read images as well as text. LLaVA-RLHF trains with a reward model plus PPO, the RL route, on picks between replies about images. RLHF-V instead collects people's corrections on short segments of a reply, where the model invents something not in the picture, and trains with dense DPO on those segments, the loss applied to each short segment on its own rather than one number for the whole reply.
